This game is clunky, unintuitive, frustrating, and unfair. It is also one of the best racers I've ever played, and definitely the best in the anti-gravity racing genre.

When I say "anti-gravity racing", it's possible that you might think of games like wipeout, redout, pacer, f-zero, ballisticNG and the like. This is a pretty unfair comparison... for those other games. You see, while most of these racing games are just essentially faster, driftier variations of car racers with maybe some pitch control gimmick, Vector 36 goes all the way in the opposite direction, going for a simmy, incredibly complex experience more akin to [i]very[/i] low flying spacecraft. Forget about crazy loop-de-looping flat tracks, you are now ripping ass through the uneven, craggy Martian circuits these hovercraft were designed for. There are no split-second, twitchy turns or shield management, instead you will be maneuvering your incredibly fast low-altitude missile through tracks via momentum, strategy, systems management, and physics. In a sense, this is the rallycross of its genre, if rally cars were able to fly at 500+ kmh.

It's not only the fact that you can basically trim your power to lift ratio on the go, or that you will need to make full use of rudder, roll and pitch to keep your craft precariously skimming past outcrops and obstacles, but you can also purchase, swap, install and fine tune the placement and orientation of all the components in your ship, which in turn will also affect its behavior, center of mass, thrust pitch and performance. As you climb the ranks you are perfectly able to simply race on the stock configurations of your ships, but if you [i]really[/i] want to get your hands dirty, prepare to spend hours upon hours just fine tuning your components on your garage and test runs to push your designs to their limit. Not only does V36 manage to offer a very unique experience, its complexity and granularity would already stand out even if the rest of the games in the space managed to come close to it. 

With that complexity, however, comes a good deal of frustration. The game has a pretty in-depth tutorial that tries its damn best to get you used to all aspects of controlling and building your craft, and the player is given a reasonable amount of tools to gauge how their design will run, however, it will be up to the player to learn and understand the whats and whys of everything that goes into a vehicle. This means that, if you really want to become proficient at the game, you will need to spend more time than one would prefer [i]ever so slightly[/i] tweaking a value, and doing a test run to see these changes in action. It's not like DIRT, where you are told in more or less certain terms what increasing your wheel camber will do, moving a repulsor slightly backward and outside, for example, will not only affect the lateral control of your ship but also the lift on that section, which also can alter your pitch, which can also alter its center of thrust, and this butterfly effect can end up in very frustrating moments where you're trying to improve your design, but end up making it worse. It's simply very hard to gauge total performance in the garage, and the process doesn't usually matter too much because, outside of category restrictions, buying a new craft tends to just be a net positive anyway. But when you pull off a modification and it works, it really feels awesome.

The amount of content in the game is alright. There are quite a few circuits to be run under different conditions, featuring jumps, craggy technical sections, tight caves and wide open desert runs, spanning over several formats of tournament which will reward money to be used to purchase new parts and ships. I don't have much complaint in regards to the variety offered, but I would be remiss to not kinda wish for more intermediate parts and vehicles to mess around with. For all the mind boggling variety of construction that the game allows, the 5 stock skimmers feel a bit bland and tinkering with a design, as I pointed out, tends to be more of a frustrating waste of time than it should, so it feels like a lot of its mechanical depth is locked behind this often obtuse facet. There are some custom skimmers available for purchase on the shop, but it would have been dope if you could win or buy templates from your rivals, or get them from other players in the workshop.

Vector 36 also has VR support. And honestly, it feels incredible. When it works. The sense of speed and scale is really well done and I'll be honest, I kinda can't go back to pancake mode now having tried it in VR. But the game can get super stuttery when even relatively small amounts of models are on screen, terrain does tear quite a bit on your peripheral vision, and it's generally just not pleasing to play. I stopped my last session over 2 hours ago, and my eyes still kinda hurt since, not to mention the queasiness. I have played a good bunch of VR games, so something's definitely wrong here. In addition to that, and while it makes a valiant effort to integrate VR controllers into experience, the motion controls are really uncomfortable and imprecise to use, although fortunately, you can just disable them and use either a joystick or a controller to play. 

EDIT: Having played it a couple more sessions, I would say you can actually play it for a good deal of time in one sitting, but you will probably need a day or two to get used to it.

VR aside however, the game does also have some weird technical quirks, like locking into a sound output and simply not playing any music or sounds when selecting a different one on windows, its lack of video options beyond a few simple selectors for resolution and general video effects. and its graphical performance isn't exactly great, even in pancake mode. The sense of speed is great and everything is really well modeled and thought out, although even for 2018 standards, the textures and effects already felt kind of cheap, but this is the small price to pay for the niche, complex and uncompromising uniqueness of small team indie developers that would otherwise not be possible when considering the "safer" alternatives released prior or since. I was surprised to see that the developers have kept support up with updates dating as recently as 2023, which is an incredible amount of commitment and dedication that must be mentioned.

The racing itself is really fun, and the AI will sometimes derp out, but you'll see opponents crash, lose components (oh yeah, there's an in-depth individual component damage system, did I mention that?) and nursing their damaged skimmers to pit for repairs and refuel. Likewise, if you mess up, you might need to hang in there with a repair, or even retire for that race and hope to do better down the championship.

Also the music slaps and the menu theme will live rent free in your head.

Overall, it really is a shame that V36 did not make the splash it should have among its target demographic, because it really is a truly groundbreaking videogame, with very solid fundamentals and a mind boggling amount of complexity and nuance, despite sometimes failing to fully accomodate the player into its more advanced features. It is also a shame that its VR mode is physically unpleasant to play for more than a race or two, as even today there is nothing else like it on the genre and with just a little more outreach I am sure would have managed to grow one of those cult followings that persist through the ages. All in all, it is a bit of a diamond in the rough, and a definitely unique racing game that deserves to be experienced.

It is Podracing in VR.  

But this is more than a quick cash grab taking advantage of Lucasarts/Disney completely failing at capitalizing on their IP.  

The real standout feature makes this actually more of a scifi 'land craft' building simulator with physics than anything else.  The garage gives you wide freedom to apply different components in a range of placements where you can also set the rotation of each component.

This is not just cosmetic, though;  every placement of components has mass and, based on placement and rotation, changes your craft's Center of Gravity (COG).  In turn, your lift and thrust components exert force in a VECTOR which radically changes your craft's performance based on their angle and relation to COG.  If that wasn't enough, you can also program how the thrust/lift components perform when given the various pitch/roll/yaw inputs.  

This results in a great physics simulator where based on your level of engineering a craft, you can accidentally make a dud that can't fly straight  or an amazing racer that performs with some maneuvering quirks that fit your playstyle.

It's unlike any other racing game you've played - the physics-based "Skimmers" operate like a hybrid between hovercrafts and quad-copters, with interesting and dynamic interactions with the environment.  The closer your craft is to the ground, the stronger the "lift vectors" interact with the ground, improving your maneuvering at the cost of a greater risk of crashing.  The faster your skimmer is moving, the better it cools, and so on.  No tracks, no guard-rails, no rules.

You can design your skimmers to match your own unique piloting/racing style with an astonishing amount of flexibility in controls and handling - you decide where to place your components; how you distribute your weight, and even the weight itself, directly impacts how your skimmer handles.  Beyond that, you can effectively program each of your vectors to respond to inputs exactly how you want, whether you want to turn on a dime, cling to the ground, soar overhead, or drift around corners to take advantage of extra cooling, it’s up to you.  There's a lot of trial-and-error here but MAN is it satisfying when you get your design to work just how you want.

Beyond the gameplay, for a racing game with as much physics integration as Vector boasts, the 3D modeling, textures, and maps look fantastic.  Those cockpits make me wish I had a VR headset!

Yes, Vector 36 is actually very good - the first few hours or so are a bit dry figuring out how to build and fly the basic low-powered skimmer and getting enough credits from racing to buy the next one (the Phi 90 - a lot more fun; a bit like an underpowered sports car).  Keep plugging away and eventually you get the Quill which has buckets of speed, handles well and doesn't require too much modification (I suggest a larger fuel tank and an extra radiator or two).  This machine is fun to fly and wins the races.  There is also a faster beast (that looks like a fish, moves like a fish,) but it steers - like - a - cow.

This is a different racing game (you're racing at 1000 kph through the canyons of Mars - the freakin' canyons of Mars, man!).  The skimmers have some altitude control whilst moving, but they don't fly like an aeroplane - if you go up too high you can come crashing back down with extreme rapidity.  You have a normal throttle that basically sits on full* and a booster throttle you apply as often as you can but make sure to watch your temperature - get too hot and bits fall off or worse.

There's lots of good and a little bit of annoying bad to this game.  The bad - ordinary menu interface, limited number of race courses, freezes often for Linux users (serves them right I suppose), you can lose previous craft modifications (only two craft at a time, with three versions each). 

But the good - so much good - the way the skimmers handle, multiplayer works very well, the environment, the look and feel,  the speed rush - the vibe of the thing - magnificent.

Short version; game's great, lots of fun, you buy now.

TL;DR: Excellent physics and immersive driving in contrast to unbalanced, frustrating and grindy racing career.

At first, I had one of my best gaming experience in years. After polishing my controls and finishing orientation tutorial I decided to train myself first. There are some training laps and instant races without any damage or fail penalties. Skimmer physics, original way of controls (thrust vs. bias) and overal driving immersion are just great. At least for me (HOTAS and Eyefinity with 3 monitors). Indeed, driving is hard to master, however I managed to win some instant races with small reward in credits. I felt so satisfied with this investment.

Then I went to actual racing... Well... the biggest problem is its poor balancing. NPCs are insanely fast and winning the regular race is incredibly difficult. On the other side, making single fatal mistake (or taking hit from your opponent's fireball) is quite easy. $6000 damage penalty without mercy.

So you try customizing your skimmer to improve the performance and controls. Editor is clunky, but you can get over it. Actually, it gives you plenty of possibilities with significant and realistic impact. You spend time trying, adjusting, testing and finally you decide to join the race again. BAM, another $6000 down the drain before you finish your first lap. Soon you end up with $zero or even in debt. Forget about buying high end skimmers or, at least, better parts...

You can try to earn some safe money in instant races. It is about $1000 in average, so it takes around 6 at least partly successful instant races to compensate single accident. Unfortunatelly, you cannot use your customized skimmer, just the default one. It starts to be grindy, tiresome and boring pretty soon. Also racing tracks are locked unless you progress. If you race 2-3 tracks which you managed to unlock, it wears off quite quickly.

To get your credits back, you can also reset the whole game. This deletes your racing history, and your skimmers too, so whereever you got with your customizations, you have to start over. And it also resets all your game settings (except for controls, thank god...), including video and sound settings, where volume goes to max, especially surprising in the middle of the night. But I think it is more a bug rather than the feature.

The game has huge potential, especially for its unique and excellent driving mechanics and customizations. However, the motivation for trying or even participating in races is close to zero. And, I think, races and racing career are what this game was made for. Maybe, just reducing damage penalty to 1/10, or possibility to save the game into 1-2 slots would easily solve those drawbacks.

I've sat down to write a review of this game a bunch of times, and each time I do I think that my time is better spent actually playing it. This is a hovercraft-style racing game that actually plays like you're in a repurposed mining vehicle hurtling through Martian canyons. It's got an incredible sense of presence in VR. Unlike most hover-racing games (looking at you, Wipeout), Vector 36 doesn't just take a 2d racing game and slap fancy sci-fi skins on it; you modulate thrust and lift to safely race through the 3d environment, making split-second decisions to trade between speed, altitude, and maneuverability. If you don't like the balance, you can customize and tweak your vehicle in a physics sandbox garage that sends me back and forth between test races to adjust part alignment by inches and degrees.

The downside to all this control and freedom is a cliff-steep learning curve that at times feels more like engineering homework than a video game. The road to proficiency in this thing is paved with flaming skimmer parts. Do it, though. It's worth it.

Davvero un hidden gem del mondo VR. E' diventato velocemente uno dei giochi dove spendo più tempo in VR, con Oculus CV1 funziona perfettamente, si apre anche senza steamvr. All'inizio non sarà per nulla semplice, risultando come esperienza simile a giochi come KSP ma anche altri sandbox di costruzione come besiege, scrap mechanic o altri dove il trial and error è fondamentale. I mezzi che si controllano sono una via di mezzo, come comportamento, tra quadricotteri e hovercraft anche se in realtà sfruttano il nucleo ferroso di marte per levitare magneticamente. La curva di apprendimento è abbastanza ripida sia per quanto riguarda il pilotaggio che la costruzione, ma molto gratificante, e in breve tempo vi ritrovere a sfrecciare su marte a 1000km/h. One of my favorite VR games, for sure. It's like a simulation version of Wipeout, Redout, etc. So cool skimming above the ground at 1000 mph! 

Half of the game is spent racing around the surface of Mars on, admittedly, monochromatic and very similar tracks. Still fun- and, you know, it's the surface of Mars so, I suppose, it's not that interesting. Although it is supposed to be terraformed so I would like to see trees, rivers, maybe some cities... I don't know. Scenery's not amazing but totally passable.

The other half of the game is spent in the garage trying to learn advanced aerophysics. Very intimidating, at first, but so worth it to slowly learn the various effects of weight placement, gyro power, rocket angle, etc. on your skimmer. It's a tiny bit frustrating to have to continually test the racer on the practice tracks because the testing facilities in the garage just don't work that well. But the garage is very fun and it's satisfying to tweak a skimmer to it's best performance.

Just a couple of bugs... one race is mislabeled. It says Steel League but it's actually Titanium League (trial and error to finally figure it out). Then there are two races that say you need a skimmer of greater value than X. When I make one with a greater value it says it's too cheap. When I make one of lesser value it says it's too cheap. When I make one of the same value it says it's too cheap. When I make a skimmer using every singe of the most expensive parts that can be bought it say's it's too cheap. So I just finally gave up on two of the races. But I managed to beat all the others in first place.

Which brings me to the final negative: It's a little too easy. Once you design a killer super fast supper skimmer you end up lapping all the competition several times. There aren't too many nail biting races with skimmers all around you fighting for first place. I feel like the races are mostly won in the garage.

Still, amazing game. Absolutely worth the price. Big thumbs up here.
